summary: NTPC runs power stations that make electricity and sells that electricity to contracted buyers, including companies that supply homes and businesses.
description: At a coal-fired station, coal is burned to heat water. The steam turns a turbine connected to a generator, which produces electricity. NTPC also has other types of generation, including renewable power. Electricity leaves a station through the wider network of lines before it can reach users.
money: Buyers pay under the station’s electricity agreement and pricing rules. Depending on the terms, charges can cover keeping the plant ready as well as electricity actually supplied. NTPC pays for fuel where needed, people, repairs, equipment and borrowing. Building a station uses money before it starts earning.
customers: Distribution companies buy electricity to supply households and businesses, and other utilities and contracted buyers also purchase power. NTPC’s electricity sales are different from the local company sending a household its usual electricity bill. Trading and consultancy have their own customers.
drivers: Whether stations are completed and ready to run, how much power buyers require, fuel availability and cost, plant efficiency, agreed charges, customer payments and spending on new projects.

groups.title: Power stations using fuel
groups.explanation: These turn fuel into electricity. They need a dependable fuel supply, functioning equipment and people to operate the station. They have costs even during periods when little electricity is produced.

groups.title: Renewable electricity
groups.examples: Solar, wind and hydro activities within the relevant group companies.
groups.explanation: Solar uses sunlight, wind turbines use moving air, and hydro stations use moving water to generate electricity. Weather and water conditions affect output differently from fuel-fired stations. The site also needs a usable connection to the electricity network.

groups.title: Fuel, trading and support services
groups.examples: Coal mining, power trading, consultancy and training.
groups.explanation: Coal mining supplies fuel. Trading involves buying and selling power under the relevant arrangements. Consultancy means carrying out agreed advisory or technical work. These are different jobs from operating a generating station.

groups.title: Projects for newer energy activities
groups.examples: Disclosed storage, green-hydrogen, nuclear and other development initiatives.
groups.explanation: These can involve studies, approvals, partnerships or construction rather than a running business. Check the stage before treating a development plan as electricity already being sold.

basics.title: Capacity describes what a station can do; output describes what it did
basics.text: Capacity is its ability to produce power under stated conditions. Generation is the electricity actually produced over time. A completed station can be ready but not running at full output if it is not required or cannot operate.

basics.title: Making power and carrying it are different jobs
basics.text: The station generates electricity. Transmission lines carry it over long distances, and local distribution networks take it towards customers. A new station needs these connections as well as its own equipment.

steps.title: Plan the station and its buyer arrangements
steps.text: Arrange permissions, a suitable site, fuel or renewable resources, funding and the agreement governing electricity sales.

steps.title: Build, test and connect it
steps.text: Construct the station, test the equipment and connect it to the network. Commissioning means bringing it into service under the relevant requirements.

steps.title: Operate when required
steps.text: Keep equipment ready, arrange fuel where needed and generate under network instructions and contract terms. Workers and repairs keep the station usable.

steps.title: Bill for the agreed charges and collect
steps.text: Calculate the bill under the agreement, receive payment and cover running and borrowing costs. A bill issued is not yet money received.

specifics.title: Ready to generate is different from being asked to generate
specifics.text: Availability means the plant is ready. Dispatch means the network calls for it to produce electricity. Plant load factor measures actual use of capacity over time. Read these together rather than assuming every idle period is a breakdown.

specifics.title: The price agreement controls what costs can be recovered
specifics.text: A tariff is the charge determined under the applicable agreement or rules. Some terms distinguish readiness charges from energy charges. Check conditions and allowed costs; a fuel-cost increase is not automatically reimbursed immediately.

specifics.title: Customers can owe money while construction bills continue
specifics.text: Amounts billed but not collected are receivables. NTPC still needs to pay for fuel, workers and new projects while waiting. Reported profit and funds available for the next investment can therefore differ.

watch: Are new stations ready to sell electricity?
Unfinished projects use money before normal income begins.
Separate announced, under-construction and operating capacity. Check test completion, network connection, agreed customers and the remaining work and cost.
Are stations ready and operating efficiently?
More output can still be costly if more fuel is needed.

Read availability, actual generation and fuel used for output. If the company uses heat rate, it is a measure of the fuel energy needed to produce electricity; understand its basis before comparing stations.
Which charges does the agreement allow?
Sales depend on more than the amount generated.
Read the tariff rules and power-purchase agreement, meaning the contract with the buyer. Check readiness conditions, fuel-cost recovery, incentives and disputed charges.
Payment delays can leave money tied up in customers.
Check amounts customers owe, how long they have been overdue, cash collected and provisions for amounts that may not be recovered. Compare these with billed sales.
Can new projects be funded without stretching the group?
Expansion requires money and people before it earns.
Read project spending, borrowing, interest and commitments through controlled companies and jointly owned businesses. Keep future technology targets separate from facilities actually running.
risks: Fuel shortages, breakdowns and weather conditions can reduce output or raise costs.
Pricing decisions, operating standards or disputed bills can prevent expected cost recovery.
Money can remain tied up in electricity buyers while NTPC’s own bills are due.
New projects take longer or cost more
Construction delays, price increases and unfamiliar technology can reduce what the investment earns.
context: Follow a new project beyond the announcement

A plan still needs permissions, construction, tests, a working network connection and customers who pay. These stages show why a future electricity target and a running station are different evidence about the business.
quiz: If a station is ready to run, must it be producing at full output?
No. It may not be called to generate that much. Read readiness, actual output and the payment terms together to understand the effect on earnings.

financialNotes.title: Verify scope before comparing generation businesses
financialNotes.text: Read the audited generation and other-business definitions, together with the internal-sales and other-income reconciliation. Capacity and power generation are operating measures, not revenue or profit. The reported segment result does not establish an individual plant’s net return or cash distribution.
